oil.summary: Crude benchmarks extended their powerful month-long rally on Wednesday, with Brent settling above $93 (+3.23% on the day, +20.6% on the month) and WTI at $86.90 (+2.33%), as the US-Iran conflict showed no sign of abating and Strait of Hormuz shipping disruptions continued to tighten physical supply. Asian refiners who had banked on August Middle East cargoes are now facing potential delivery delays, while Pakistan is actively scouting US, Nigerian, and Central Asian crude alternatives. A bearish counter-signal arrived via EIA data showing a 2.0 million barrel US crude inventory build for the week ending July 17, echoed by an API estimate of 2.6 million barrels. Refined products diverged sharply: Heating Oil (+31.8% on the month) reflects distillate tightness, while RBOB gasoline fell 4.17% on the day. Russia has reclaimed the top slot in India's import basket, and China's demand trajectory remains a key swing variable for the remainder of the year.
drivers: US-Iran conflict escalating with Hormuz blockage disrupting Middle East crude flows and forcing Asian and South Asian buyers to seek alternative supply
US crude inventories built 2.0–2.6 million barrels in the week to July 17, providing a modest bearish offset to geopolitical risk premium
Russia displacing Iranian barrels in India's import mix; China's import pace and refined product exports flagged as the key price swing factor through year-end

gas.summary: European and US natural gas markets are diverging sharply. TTF surged 4.58% on the day to €62.40/MWh, extending a stunning 48.96% monthly gain, as Equinor CEO Anders Opedal warned on Wednesday that European storage is unlikely to reach even 80% capacity before the onset of winter — the weakest pre-winter cushion in 15 years. That supply anxiety is compounded by the broader Middle East crisis squeezing LNG and pipeline flows into Europe. US Henry Hub, by contrast, gained a modest 1.71% to $2.914/MMBtu but remains down 10.42% on the month, reflecting looser domestic fundamentals. Equinor reported a 93% jump in Q2 profit, crediting the oil and gas price spike driven by the Middle East crisis. Gas-sector data in today's feed is otherwise limited.
drivers: Equinor CEO warned European storage will likely remain below 80% ahead of winter, the lowest pre-season buffer in 15 years, pushing TTF to a +48.96% monthly gain
Middle East conflict and Hormuz disruptions adding risk premium to European LNG and pipeline supply expectations
Henry Hub diverging lower from TTF (-10.42% on the month), reflecting comparatively ample US domestic supply

power.summary: Power and carbon markets are feeling the full heat of the energy price shock. EU Carbon EUAs rose 3.72% on the day to $81.53, up 6.47% on the month, likely tracking higher gas and oil costs that are reducing the economic appeal of fuel-switching and sustaining coal and gas burn in European grids. Japan's day-ahead electricity prices hit a three-and-a-half-year high on Wednesday, driven by soaring fuel costs, a heat wave, and a weakening currency, per today's headlines. The broader backdrop is one of structural fossil-fuel dependency: the Energy Institute's latest Statistical Review confirmed that fossil fuels still generate 57% of global electricity. Equinor's 93% Q2 profit surge, attributable to the Middle East-driven commodity spike, illustrates the windfall flowing to producers at the expense of power consumers. Specific EU power price data was not provided today.
drivers: Japan's day-ahead spot electricity prices surged to a 3.5-year high, driven by soaring fuel costs, a heat wave, and yen weakness
EU EUAs gained 3.72% on the day as elevated gas prices limit fuel-switching and keep carbon-intensive generation economically active
Energy Institute data confirms fossil fuels account for 57% of global electricity generation, underlining systemic exposure to the current commodity price shock
